In [[algebra]], a '''linear Lie algebra''' is a subalgebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> of the [[Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{gl}(V)</math> consisting of [[endomorphism]]s of a [[vector space]] ''V''. In other words, a linear Lie algebra is the image of a [[Lie algebra representation]].

Any Lie algebra is a linear Lie algebra in the sense that there is always a faithful representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> (in fact, on a [[dimension (vector space)|finite-dimensional]] vector space by [[Ado's theorem]] if <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is itself finite-dimensional.)

Let ''V'' be a finite-dimensional vector space over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] zero and <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> a subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak{gl}(V)</math>. Then ''V'' is semisimple as a module over <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> if and only if (i) it is a direct sum of the center and a semisimple ideal and (ii) the elements of the center are [[diagonalizable matrix|diagonalizable]] (over some [[extension field]]).<ref>{{harvnb|Jacobson|1979|loc=Ch III, Theorem 10}}</ref>
